Congress’s tendency to delegate more or less discretion varies over time 
depending on the natui’e of problems lawmakers face and the political 
chcumstances in which they operate. One sometimes hears a stylized narrative 
that delegation has been ever increasing, but history is actually a more 
complicated and chaotic mix of ebbs and flows. Nor does greater delegation 
necessai’ily mean more regulatory intervention in the market. To be sure, 
regulatoiy laws of the New Deal era often lived up to their reputation as both 
interventionist and discretionaiy. E.g., Robert L. Rabin, Federal Regulation in 
Historical Perspective, 38 Stan. L. Rev. 1189 (1986). But the outpouring of 
environmental legislation from 1970 through 1990 was interventionist yet 
often relatively nozi-discretionary, thanks in part to the fact that Democrats so 
often controlled Congress in the face of a Republican White House they 
distrusted. One study of environmental legislation during the 1980s 
documented a clear trend in the direction of tightened statutory control over 
the content and timetable of administrative implementation. See Sidney A. 
Shapiro & Robert L. Glicksman, Congress, the Supreme Court, and the Quiet 
Revolution in Administrative Law, 1988 Du k e L.J. 819. A further illustration 
IS provided by the 1990 amendments to the Clean Air Act, which specified 
precisely the amount of pollutant reduction that each of several hundred 
named sources of emissions had to achieve. It would not be far-fetched to claim 
that the statute constituted EPA’s regulations.

what are they? The Constitution contemplates that Congress will exercise
